questions.question: Which statement best describes encapsulation in object-oriented programming?
options: Bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single class, while restricting direct access to the object's internals
Defining several methods in one class that share a name but take different parameter lists
Creating a new class that automatically receives all the fields and methods of an existing class
Splitting a large program into many small source files so each class is easier to find
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is two moves made together: bundle state and behaviour into one unit (the class), and hide the state so all access goes through methods you choose to expose. Same-name methods and receiving members from another class describe overloading and inheritance, which are different ideas.

questions.question: Which list names the four major principles (pillars) of object-oriented programming?
options: Compilation, inheritance, iteration, abstraction
Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction
Encapsulation, instantiation, iteration, recursion
Classes, objects, methods, variables
questions.explanation: OOP rests on four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction. Encapsulation comes first because the other three build on classes that protect their own data. Classes, objects and methods are building blocks of the language, not principles.

questions.question: One pillar of OOP is summed up as: objects guard their own data behind a small public face. Which pillar is it?
options: Inheritance
Polymorphism
Abstraction
Encapsulation
questions.explanation: Guarding an object's own state behind a controlled public interface is encapsulation. Inheritance builds new classes on existing ones, polymorphism lets one method call produce many behaviours, and abstraction exposes what something does while hiding how it works.

questions.question: What does the term data hiding mean in the context of encapsulation?
options: Encrypting field values before they are stored in memory
Making fields private so code outside the class cannot access them directly
Declaring fields inside methods so that other methods cannot see them
Giving fields deliberately obscure names so other programmers leave them alone
questions.explanation: Data hiding is the hiding half of encapsulation: fields are made private, so the only way in is through the methods the class chooses to expose. It is access control enforced by the compiler, not encryption or naming tricks.

questions.question: What is the standard two-step recipe for encapsulating the state of a Java class?
options: Declare the fields public and add comments warning other programmers not to misuse them
Declare the fields static and access them through the class name instead of an object
Declare the fields protected and read them only from subclasses
Declare the fields private and provide a public getter and setter method for each one
questions.explanation: The recipe is mechanical: make every instance variable private, then expose controlled access through public getters and setters. Comments carry no enforcement, and static changes sharing rather than visibility; only private makes the compiler block outside access.

questions.question: Which access modifier makes a class member accessible only from code inside that same class?
options: protected
public
private
default (writing no modifier keyword)
questions.explanation: private is the strictest level: only the class's own code can touch the member. Default opens it to the whole package, protected adds subclasses in other packages, and public opens it to everywhere.

questions.question: Getter and setter methods also have formal names. What are they?
options: Getters are accessor methods; setters are mutator methods
Getters are mutator methods; setters are accessor methods
Getters and setters are both known as constructor methods
Getters are called iterators; setters are called initialisers
questions.explanation: A getter accesses (reads) the current value of a private field, so it is an accessor; a setter mutates (updates) the value, so it is a mutator. Constructors are a separate mechanism that initialises a brand-new object.

questions.question: A class declares the field: private String email; Following standard Java naming conventions, what is its getter called?
options: email()
readEmail()
Email()
getEmail()
questions.explanation: The convention is the prefix get or set followed by the field name with its first letter capitalised: getEmail() and setEmail(...). IDEs generate exactly these names, and other Java programmers and libraries rely on the pattern.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Nothing - it fails to compile because speed is private
The program compiles but crashes with an exception at run time
questions.explanation: Main never touches the private field directly; it goes through the public setter and getter, which is exactly the access encapsulation intends. setSpeed(100) stores 100 in the field and getSpeed() reads it back.

questions.question: What happens when you try to compile and run this code?
options: It fails to compile: balance has private access in Account
It compiles and runs, and balance becomes 50.0
It compiles, but throws an exception at run time when balance is assigned
It compiles with a warning, and balance keeps its default value 0.0
questions.explanation: private means only code inside Account may touch balance, so the assignment in Main is rejected by the compiler. That is the point: an illegal write is caught at compile time, before the program can ever run with bad data.

questions.question: A field is declared as: int count; with no access modifier keyword. From where can it be accessed directly?
options: Only from code in the same class
From the same class and from any class in the same package
From the same class, its package, and subclasses in other packages
From anywhere in the program
questions.explanation: Writing no keyword gives default (package) access: the class itself plus every class in the same package. Even subclasses are excluded once they live in another package; that extra reach requires protected. Forgetting private therefore silently opens a field to its whole package.

questions.question: Which access level allows a member to be used from its own class, its package, and subclasses in other packages, but not from unrelated classes elsewhere?
options: private
default (no modifier)
protected
public
questions.explanation: protected is package access plus subclasses: even a subclass in a different package may use the member. Only public opens a member to all code everywhere, and default stops at the package boundary.

questions.question: Java is often described as having three access modifier keywords but four levels of access. What explains the difference?
options: The fourth level, default (package) access, has no keyword: it applies when you write no modifier at all
The static keyword acts as a fourth access modifier when it is placed before a field
protected counts twice because it behaves differently for fields and for methods
private and public can be combined on one member to produce an intermediate level
questions.explanation: The keywords are private, protected and public; the fourth level, default (package) access, is what you get by writing nothing. static is not an access modifier, protected has a single meaning, and access modifiers can never be combined.

questions.question: Counter and Till are two classes in the same package. What happens when this code is compiled and run?
options: Compile error: count has private access in Counter
Compile error: every field must be given an access modifier
It compiles and prints 5
It compiles, but an exception is thrown when count is assigned
questions.explanation: A field with no modifier has default (package) access, so every class in the same package may use it directly. Till and Counter share the package shop, so the access is legal and 5 is printed. Default is looser than private; only private would have blocked this.

questions.question: A setter that simply assigns its parameter to the field looks no better than a public field. What real advantage does routing all access through getter and setter methods still provide?
options: Method calls are optimised by the compiler, so access through getters is faster than field access
Validation or a new internal data representation can be added later without changing any calling code
Getters and setters allow several objects to share a single copy of the field's value
The compiler refuses to accept a private field unless a getter and a setter are provided
questions.explanation: Even an empty setter is a checkpoint you can staff later: the day rules are needed, you add them in one place and not one caller changes. A public field can never be upgraded that way. There is no speed benefit, and the compiler never demands getters or setters.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: theRedRhino
An empty string
It throws a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time
theRedRhin
questions.explanation: The argument has 11 characters, so the setter's guard runs substring(0, 10) and stores only the first ten: theRedRhin. The validation happens invisibly inside the setter, so the caller never has to check and no code anywhere can store an 11-character username.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: ada@example.com
null
It fails to compile: the variable email is already defined in setEmail
An empty string
questions.explanation: Inside the setter the parameter name shadows the field, so email = email assigns the parameter to itself and the field is never written; the String field keeps its default value null. Writing this.email = email is what stores the parameter in the field, because this. breaks the tie when the names clash.

questions.question: How do you make a private field readable from outside the class but impossible for outside code to overwrite?
options: Provide a public getter for it, but no public setter
Provide a public setter for it, but no public getter
Change its access modifier from private to protected
Keep it private and add a comment stating that it is read-only
questions.explanation: A getter with no setter splits reading from writing: the world may look, but changes can only happen through whatever controlled methods the class itself offers. A field exposed directly is all-or-nothing; whoever can read it can also write it.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: drive(30) and drive(20) pass the distance > 0 guard; drive(-10) fails it and is silently ignored, so km ends at 50. Because the class offers no setter, km is read-only from outside and can only legally increase through drive().

questions.question: A Person class stores middle names internally as one String. It is rewritten so the private field becomes a String array, while getMiddleNames() still returns a String and setMiddleNames(String) still accepts one; both public signatures are unchanged. What happens to existing code that uses Person?
options: Every caller must be rewritten, because the field's type changed from String to an array
Callers still compile, but the getter now returns null because the internal type changed
Callers fail at run time when the internal array cannot be converted back to a String
Callers keep compiling and running unchanged, because they depend only on the method signatures
questions.explanation: Callers bind to the public methods, not the private internals. The getter joins the array back into one String on the way out and the setter splits the incoming String on the way in, so from outside nothing observable changed. This freedom to rebuild the insides is a core benefit of encapsulation.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: deposit(-50) fails the amount > 0 guard and withdraw(500) fails amount <= balance, so both are silently ignored; only deposit(25) passes, leaving 100.0 + 25 = 125.0. The guards inside the methods keep the object valid without the caller doing anything.

questions.question: Which line, if any, fails to compile?
options: Line 1, because deposit() changes a private field
Line 2, because a private field cannot be read from outside the class in any way
Line 3, because balance has private access in BankAccount
None of them; all three lines compile
questions.explanation: Code inside BankAccount may use its own private field freely, and lines 1 and 2 go through public methods, which is exactly the intended interface. Only line 3 names the private field directly from another class, so only it is rejected by the compiler.

questions.question: In a very large program, a public field such as balance is written with a wildly wrong value by one forgotten line. Why is this bug so hard to track down?
options: Assigning to a field runs no code, so nothing can validate, log, or break on the change, and every line able to reach the field is a suspect
Public fields are kept in a protected memory area that debuggers are not permitted to inspect
The JVM batches field assignments together, so the write happens at an unpredictable moment
The compiler removes field assignments from stack traces, so the responsible line cannot appear in them
questions.explanation: Assignment is not an event: no method runs when a public field is written, so there is no single place to validate, log, or set a breakpoint, and any code that can see the field could be the culprit. Forcing every change through one setter gives one door, one guard, and one place to look.

questions.question: In an IDE you create a Student object in another class and type student. to open the autocomplete list. The field gpa used to appear in that list, but it no longer does, even though the field still exists under the same name. What most likely changed?
options: The field was moved below the methods in the Student source file
The field's access modifier was changed from public to private
The class was recompiled with a newer version of Java
The getter method for gpa was deleted, which hides the field itself from the list
questions.explanation: The autocomplete list shows only members that are accessible from the calling code, so making a field private removes it from the list outside its own class. If you cannot see it in the list, you cannot access it directly; the IDE is surfacing Java's access rules.

questions.question: A class must enforce that age stays between 16 and 100, both when an object is constructed and whenever setAge() is called later. What is the recommended way to implement this without duplicating the rule?
options: Validate only in the constructor, since an object cannot become invalid after it has been created
Make the field public so that each caller becomes responsible for validating values itself
Write the rule once in a private helper method and call it from both the constructor and the setter
Copy the validation code into both places, because a constructor is not allowed to call other methods
questions.explanation: A constructor is a kind of setter too: it sets the fields' first values, so it needs the same rule as setAge(). A private helper such as validateAge() holds the logic once, following the DRY principle, and both entry points call it. Skipping either entry point would let invalid data in.

questions.question: A class's constructor and setter both call a shared validateAge() helper method. Why should that helper be declared private rather than public?
options: private methods are compiled to faster bytecode than public methods
Java requires every method that a constructor calls to be declared private
Declaring it private prevents the helper from being called more than once per object
The helper is internal machinery for the class's own use, not an operation the class means to offer callers
questions.explanation: A class's public members should be exactly the operations it intends the outside world to use. The validation rule is an internal detail supporting the constructor and setter, so it stays hidden and can change freely without affecting any caller. Access modifiers say nothing about speed or how often a method may run.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: 150 then 21
16 then 21
16 then 16
150 then 16
questions.explanation: The constructor routes 150 through the shared private helper, which rejects anything outside 16 to 100 and returns 16, so the object starts in a valid state and the first line prints 16. setAge(21) passes the same check, so the second line prints 21.

questions.question: The scores field is private. What does this program print?
options: 70, because a private field cannot be changed from outside its class
It fails to compile: view[0] = 0 writes to a private array
It throws an exception at run time when view[0] is assigned
questions.explanation: The getter returns a reference to the internal array, not a copy, so view and the private scores variable point at the same object and view[0] = 0 rewrites the private data. private seals the field itself, not the object it refers to; a capsule leaks if its getters hand out references to internal mutable state.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: It fails to compile: Arrays.copyOf cannot be applied to a private field
questions.explanation: Arrays.copyOf hands the caller a brand-new array, a defensive copy, so view[0] = 0 scribbles on the copy while the private original stays 70, 80, 90. The second getScores() call copies the untouched original, so element 0 is still 70.

questions.question: What does this code print?
options: ADA then ADA
ada then ADA
ada then ada
ADA then ada
questions.explanation: String is immutable, a capsule with no write gates: toUpperCase() cannot change the original, so it returns a new String instead. name still refers to ada while loud refers to the new ADA; that unchangeability is what makes Strings safe to share anywhere.

questions.question: Why can a public field never provide the flexibility to swap a class's internal data representation, while a getter and setter pair can?
options: Public fields are allocated on the stack, and stack storage cannot change its layout
The compiler permanently locks the declared type of any field marked public
Callers bind directly to the field's type, so changing it breaks them; a method commits only to its signature, leaving the body free to change
Public fields cannot store arrays or other object types, so there is nothing to swap
questions.explanation: With a public field, the field's type is the public contract: change it and every access point breaks. A method promises only its signature, so its body can translate between the published parameter and return types and any internal representation, and callers never notice.

questions.question: A team replaces a public balance field with a private field plus guarded deposit and withdraw methods. A forgotten line elsewhere still contains: account.balance = -1000000; In debugging terms, what has making the field private achieved?
options: The bad write still happens, but the JVM now logs a warning each time that line runs
The bad write becomes a run-time exception instead of silently corrupting the balance
Nothing changes until a public setter is also written for the balance field
The bad write becomes a compile-time error, caught before the program can even be run
questions.explanation: With the field private, the stray assignment no longer compiles (balance has private access), so the bug moves from run time, where a victim finds it weeks later, to compile time, where the programmer finds it instantly. Encapsulation makes the invalid write impossible rather than merely detectable.
